questions.question: A producer function only sends and a consumer only receives — how do you enforce that in Go?
questions.title: Channel Direction Scenario
questions.direct_answer: Use directional types in the signatures: producer takes chan<- T (send-only), consumer takes <-chan T (receive-only). The compiler rejects the wrong direction — the contract is in the type.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Use directional types in the signatures: producer takes chan<- T (send-only), consumer takes <-chan T (receive-only). The compiler rejects the wrong direction — the contract is in the type.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The enforcement:

```go
func producer(out chan<- int) {  // send-only — can't receive from out
    for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
        out <- i
    }
    close(out)  // close is a SENDER operation — legal on chan<-
}

func consumer(in <-chan int) {  // receive-only — can't send to in, can't close
    for v := range in {
        fmt.Println(v)
    }
}

// main creates the bidirectional channel and passes it:
ch := make(chan int)
go producer(ch)  // implicit conversion: chan int → chan<- int
go consumer(ch) // implicit conversion: chan int → <-chan int
```

What the direction types enforce, via the compiler:
- <-out in producer: compile error (receive on send-only)
- in <- 1 in consumer: compile error (send on receive-only)
- close(in) in consumer: compile error (close is sender-owned)

The conversion is one-way: bidirectional → directional is automatic; directional back to bidirectional is impossible. Once narrowed to a view, the view stays narrow — the caller (holding the bidirectional original) retains all operations.

The API-design pattern: producers return <-chan T (the caller can only consume); consumers accept chan<- T (the caller hands over the feeding rights). The direction in the signature IS the ownership documentation, enforced.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[chan int bidirectional] --> P[chan<- int: producer sends]
    B --> C[<-chan int: consumer receives]
    P -->|close ok| P2[sender owns lifecycle]
    C -->|close: compile error| C2[receiver never closes]
    B -->|implicit conversion| P
    B -->|implicit conversion| C
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics: chan<- T and <-chan T are distinct types in the type system. The conversion (bidirectional → directional) is implicit — the runtime value is unchanged (the same channel pointer), only the compile-time view narrows. The compiler removes the forbidden operations at build time — a direction misuse is a compile error, never a runtime surprise.

The close ownership, formally: close broadcasts 'no more values' to every receiver — a decision only the sender can make (only it knows when production ends). The type system aligns: close is defined on chan<- T and the bidirectional chan T — NOT on <-chan T. A consumer can never close, structurally.

The pattern that composes into pipelines: stage(in <-chan int, out chan<- int) — each stage consumes read-only, produces write-only, and the lifecycle close (defer close(out)) belongs to the stage with the send authority — the channel-direction + close-ownership + defer pattern is the complete Go pipeline discipline.
